transcript_body:
Meeting header: 2026-03-23 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~54m | Attendees: Liam Carter, Priya Nair (Redwood); Sophie Park, Marco Ruiz, Ethan Cole, Clara Zhao (Talon Metrics)

[00:00] Liam Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, I'm Liam, i'm the AE on the account, with Priya on the SE side. Sophie, Marco, Ethan, Clara, thanks for taking the time.
[00:10] Sophie Park: Hi Liam, thanks. We wanted to spend most of the time on cost economics — we've been running a couple prototypes with other vendors and want to understand where Redwood lands on per-token plus infra.
[00:18] Priya Nair: great. we'll cover hosted vs dedicated vs private and then dig into batching/caching levers. If at any point stop me — we're happy to go deep.
[00:26] Marco Ruiz: quick context — we're doing an extractive summarization flow on financial filings, ~16k context, median response size 2k tokens, expected QPS during peak 8-12 reqs/s but spikes to ~25 for a few hours. Budget for pilot is tight, aiming for under $15k/month for inference initially.
[00:44] Ethan Cole: and security: we need KMS-integrated encryption and audit logs; private deployment is on the table but adds time.
[00:52] Liam Carter: understood. at a high level: Hosted = simple per-token billing, fastest to start; Dedicated = reserved GPU pools, better unit economics at scale and stable latency; Private = customer-managed VPC/on-prem, enterprise security but longer lead time and platform fee.
[01:08] Sophie Park: can you give us example numbers? ballpark per-token for hosted and what dedicated looks like?
[01:15] Priya Nair: yes, caveat this is illustrative. for a high-quality 16k-context open model we typically see hosted egress-inference in the $0.0035 - $0.006 per 1k output-token range depending on model and peak shaping. that includes stateless hosted serving, not reserved capacity.
[01:34] Priya Nair: Dedicated reserved capacity usually lowers raw per-token by around 25-50% for heavy steady workloads because you amortize GPU cost. plus you can use more aggressive batching and quantization profiles which further reduce cost.
[01:47] Marco Ruiz: 25-50% is a wide range. what's driving it?
[01:51] Priya Nair: it depends on utilization and model family. if you have consistent 70-90% GPU utilization on a pool, the cost amortization is strong. if you're 10-20% utilization, Dedicated can be worse. also batching profiles - if you can tolerate slightly higher median latency, batching packs more tokens per GPU run reducing per-token kernel overhead.
[02:10] Clara Zhao: how much latency penalty are we talking about if we batch aggressively? our SLO is p95 < 800ms during peak.
[02:18] Priya Nair: with continuous batching we can keep p95 under 800ms for many configs, but it depends on sequence lengths and concurrency. for 16k context, we often recommend a hybrid: micro-batching for latency-sensitive routes and larger batch windows for high-throughput backfills. you'd see maybe +100-300ms in median for the bigger batch windows, but tail depends on queuing.
[02:39] Sophie Park: caching — you mentioned KV/prefix caching earlier in the email. can that help our summarization use case? a lot of filings have repeated boilerplate sections.
[02:48] Priya Nair: yes. prefix and KV cache works well if requests share prefixes or have reuse in the KV stage; for summarization, if you chunk docs and reuse embeddings or partial KV states across requests, we can save substantial token work. conservative expectation is 10-30% token reduction for moderate reuse; if you have high reuse it can be 40% or more.
[03:07] Marco Ruiz: ok interesting. what's needed from our side to estimate that?
[03:11] Priya Nair: we need a representative prompt set with token counts and any repeat patterns. Sophie if you can share a week's worth of requests (anonymized) we'll run a caching sensitivity analysis.
[03:20] Sophie Park: yes we can.
[03:22] Ethan Cole: about private deployment — we have a procurement window of ~8 weeks. If we go private, how does that change costs? is it mostly a platform fee plus infra?
[03:31] Liam Carter: private typically is a platform fee plus the cost of the underlying infra you bring; Redwood can quote a private license and provide an on-prem package. Private can reduce per-token costs if you self-provision at high utilization but there's ops overhead. For most pilots we recommend Hosted or Dedicated first.
[03:45] Clara Zhao: finance question — how predictable is billing on Dedicated? we prefer predictable monthly commits rather than wild per-token swings.
[03:53] Priya Nair: Dedicated is ideal for predictability — you commit to a reserved pool size/month and get predictable unit costs. We also support burst-to-hosted policies so you don't drop requests if you exceed the pool. That hybrid affects unit economics but gives uptime guarantees.
[04:08] Marco Ruiz: can you show a simple cost model? e.g., given our expected QPS and token sizes, what's hosted vs dedicated monthly?
[04:15] Liam Carter: yes -- action item: we'll build a tailored spreadsheet. rough back-of-envelope, using your numbers: average output 2k tokens, input ~14k, total tokens per request 16k. at peak average 10 rps sustained, that's 10 * 16k * 3600 * 24 * 30 = huge number — sorry that's per-second math, let me frame it per month: 10 reqs/s * 3600 * 24 * 30 ~ 25,920,000 requests/month; times 16k tokens -> ~414 billion tokens/month. that seems off for a pilot—are we sure about 10 sustained rps?
[05:00] Sophie Park: no, that's peak QPS across a model used by multiple products; our pilot will be a gated fraction — estimate 800k-1.5M requests/month for the pilot.
[05:10] Liam Carter: OK good, that changes things. 1M requests * 16k tokens = 16 billion tokens. at hosted $0.004 per 1k output tokens (approx) that's about $64k for output tokens alone — again depends on how vendor splits input vs output metering.
[05:28] Priya Nair: two notes: 1) many vendors meter only output tokens or charge different rates for input vs output, and 2) batching + quantization + KV caching can reduce effective token work substantially. if you can reduce token work by 50% via caching/long-context optimizations, that hosted bill looks like $32k.
[05:45] Clara Zhao: but that's still above pilot budget. is Dedicated viable for 16B token equivalent at that scale?
[05:52] Priya Nair: Dedicated could be much cheaper if we can size a pool that hits high utilization. for example, a 4x A100-equivalent pool with reserved commit might cost Xk/month and support your throughput at a per-token cost 30-45% lower than hosted. I'll avoid quoting exact $ without the sizing run.
[06:10] Marco Ruiz: what's turnaround on a sizing run?
[06:12] Priya Nair: if you share requests and token distribution, we can run a perf estimate within 48-72 hours — we'll simulate batching and KV caching effects.
[06:21] Sophie Park: ok we'll share samples post call.
[06:24] Ethan Cole: what about quantization? we have some float sensitivity concerns — quality is important for compliance.
[06:30] Priya Nair: we recommend mixed approach: run evals of quantized model variants against your prompt/eval set. some models are resilient to int8/4-bit quantization for inference; we can provide recommendations and a quick A/B on output similarity metrics. quantization usually reduces cost by 10-30% depending on model and hardware.
[06:49] Marco Ruiz: can Redwood run those evals or do we need to do them?
[06:53] Priya Nair: we can run them as part of a pilot; we'll need sample prompts and any reference labels. it's a standard deliverable in our PoC package.
[07:02] Clara Zhao: security question — for Hosted, do you support customer-managed KMS?
[07:07] Liam Carter: yes, Hosted supports envelope encryption with customer-managed KMS keys (AWS KMS, GCP KMS) for objects and audit logging. we'll attach SOC2 artifacts in the pack.
[07:16] Sophie Park: any gotchas around PII in logs? we need log redaction and retention controls.
[07:21] Priya Nair: we have retention policies and can redact or disable logging at token-level; for the pilot we often disable full transcript logging and only keep minimal traces.
[07:31] Ethan Cole: ok operationally, if we start on Hosted and then move to Dedicated, what's the migration path?
[07:36] Liam Carter: same API and model configs, you can pin model versions and move routing policies; it's mainly configuration and capacity provisioning on our side. we do customer migrations regularly.
[07:45] Sophie Park: timeline for Dedicated provision?
[07:48] Priya Nair: for standard Dedicated pools it's about 2-3 weeks for provisioning and initial autoscale config; Private adds more time.
[07:56] Marco Ruiz: question on burst-to-hosted: how is the cost accounted? if we reserve capacity but burst to hosted during peaks, do we pay both?
[08:03] Liam Carter: you pay the reserved commit plus hosted egress for the burst usage; we try to size pools and burst policies to minimize double-spend. some contracts include blended pricing for a short period.
[08:15] Clara Zhao: any examples of customers that saved >30% moving from hosted to dedicated?
[08:19] Priya Nair: yes, several fintechs with predictable throughput moved to Dedicated and saw 35-50% reduction in $/token after batching and quantization. I'll add anonymized case studies.
[08:30] Sophie Park: are there any minimum commitments for Dedicated?
[08:33] Liam Carter: typically monthly reserved commits with flexible scaling; we can structure pilot-friendly minimal commits if you want to test.
[08:40] Marco Ruiz: okay, can we get a modeled spreadsheet that shows Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private with assumptions for caching percent, quantization savings, and utilization?
[08:48] Liam Carter: yes, we'll send a spreadsheet with toggles for caching %, quantization %, utilization, and pilot vs scale numbers.
[08:55] Priya Nair: and we'll include a perf estimate run for your sample prompts.
[08:59] Sophie Park: great. last thing: our procurement/contact is on a tight timeline — if we like the pilot numbers, we could sign a small dedicated commit.
[09:07] Liam Carter: noted. we'll aim to get you pricing + perf analysis by Wednesday (2026-03-25).
[09:12] Marco Ruiz: thanks. a couple small transcription notes — the team sometimes calls 'KV cache' as 'K V cache' or 'key value caching' so apologies for any mismatches in naming.
[09:21] Liam Carter: no worries. any final Qs?
[09:24] Ethan Cole: none from me.
[09:26] Sophie Park: that's it, thanks Liam, Priya.
[09:28] Liam Carter: thanks everyone — recap in the doc: we'll send pricing spreadsheet, perf estimate after prompt samples, schedule dedicated demo if pilot looks good.
[09:36] End of transcript.
